## Welcome!

I'm Wilson, a postdoc within the [Center for the Experimental-Philosophical Study of Discrimination (CEPDISC)](https://cepdisc.au.dk/) at Aarhus University (Denmark) and guest researcher in the Department of Psychology at the University of Oslo (Norway). I received my PhD in social psychology from the University of Michigan in 2024.

A coworker's Hermès bag, a Whole Foods in a gentrifying neighborhood, and a stranger's Yankees hat each offer clues to social rank and group identity. We decode cues like these effortlessly because navigating hierarchies — group-based asymmetries in rank, resources, and influence — is one of the fundamental social problems the mind is equipped to solve. My research traces the signatures of a shared cognitive framework for reading hierarchy across three levels at which social life is organized: the *places* we inhabit, the *faces* we perceive, and the *groups* we belong to. A parallel program extends this same attention to consensual, cross-cultural regularities into a different domain: how people manage one of social life's oldest threats, infectious illness.

In the hierarchy program, I ask how the spatial clustering of resources ("patchiness") shapes perceptions of *places*, how reverse-correlated visual templates reveal who people picture as rich, poor, or powerful in their *faces*, and how coalition boundaries are drawn and contested among *groups*, with a focus on multiracial Americans. Across all three levels, I find a striking degree of consensus in these perceptions, often independent of political ideology.

The disease program centers on concealment: the widespread, cross-culturally consistent tendency to hide signs of one's own illness from others. I'm now working to quantify its consequences for disease spread and to test interventions that reduce it.

Across both programs, I favor methods that reveal what people perceive rather than what they report — geospatial mapping, visual reverse correlation, and agent-based modeling — and draw on behavioral ecology, evolutionary biology, and political science to explain why these patterns emerge, with an emphasis on populations beyond the usual samples.

See the [Research](research.qmd) tab for publications.

I have also been fortunate to teach and mentor many students in both classroom and lab settings. My pedagogical interests include equity-focused research methods teaching, debunking psychology myths, and examining evolutionary psychology in undergraduate curricula. See [Teaching & Mentoring](teaching-mentoring.qmd) for more.

Prior to my postdoctoral position and graduate studies, I received a BA in Economics and Psychology from Macalester College (Saint Paul, MN) and worked as a research analyst at The Brattle Group (Washington, DC). I grew up in Poughkeepsie, NY, a place primarily known for one of the longest walking bridges in the world, Vassar College, and an episode of *Friends*.
